### Distributed and peer-to-peer systems

<!-- Don't love it but we needed something. Also does this go here or in the above section? Ugh. -->
<!-- lmao yet another definition of (distributed) system -->
We will define a _system_ as an overarching container of programs and protocols that does something when put together. A system could just be a single program on a single device. But it can also span multiple programs and computers. For example, the Internet Protocol (IP) is a system that allows computers to reach and communicate with each other even when they're not directly connected.
<!-- We will define a "system" as one or more programs running on one or more devices connected by some network which collectively act as part of some larger service. -->

TODO should I explain client-server right here?

The client-server model with a single server runs into scaling issues: no computer of today, regardless of how much processing power it has or how much bandwidth its network has, could possibly handle all of the requests that are demanded upon some services (e.g. a single computer serving all Google search results). As such, the work of handling all these requests must be managed amongst multiple computers.
A _distributed system_ is a system as defined above where multiple devices work together to provide some program or service, instead of one machine doing it all. [@distsys-textbook p. 2]

An old example of a distributed system is Grapevine [@grapevine], an early email service. Xerox had local electronic mail servers in its offices, and the workstations were connected to some local server; the servers were also connected to each other via telephone lines. Given this setup, Grapevine was designed to facilitate email getting from one workstation to another regardless of their location.
There were components for email delivery, authenictation, and so on, and each had to deal with its own challenges due to the distributed nature of the system. For example if the dial-up connection between two offices is down, what should the email-fetcher do --- stall until the line is back, or try again in an hour? These are the sorts of problems that come up with unreliable networks.

A _peer-to-peer_ system is a special kind of distributed system.
For the First International Conference on Peer-to-Peer Computing, peer-to-peer is defined as when
"the participants share a part of their own hardware resources ... These shared resources are necessary to provide the Service ... [and] are accessible by other peers directly, without passing intermediary entities. The participants of such a network are thus ... providers and ... requestors" [@p2p].
They additionally define "pure" peer-to-peer with the additional constraint that any single node can be removed without impacting service, and the network is "hybrid" otherwise.
<!-- don't love this direct quotation but it works for now. Come back later -->

This is a complex definition and already shows the nuances of peer-to-peer systems. Most of the time, peer-to-peer is defined in contrast to a client-server architecture --- instead of marking a computer as either a client that requests data or server that responds to requests, all machines are equal in some sense and can operate as both clients and servers. A simple example of a peer-to-peer program is BitTorrent [@sam-thesis], which is used for file sharing: a node both downloads data from other nodes and provides data for upload to other nodes. This provides resilience, reduced load, and increased speed when many devices would otherwise all have to request the data from the same server.

Note that the line between client-server and peer-to-peer gets messy. For example, Dynamo [@dynamo] is a system from Amazon to provide a key-value store. The entire system operates as a server for external clients: a device can connect to some machine in the Dynamo system and ask for the value corresponding to some key. However, amongst the Dynamo servers the protocol is peer-to-peer --- no Dynamo node is structurally prioritized over another.

### Challenges with distributed and peer-to-peer systems

Distributed and peer-to-peer systems have many challenges that need to be worked around [@distsys-textbook, p. 30].
Since the network can fail, there are many problems that plague all distributed systems: messages can be delayed, dropped, corrupted, delivered out-of-order, and duplicated.
Since network partitions could happen anywhere and at any time, nodes can become instantaneously unreachable, including partway through communication.

And there are additional difficulties associated with peer-to-peer networks.
In many settings a peer-to-peer system is _open_, meaning that nodes are free to join or leave at any point in time.
For example, a new user can set up a BitTorrent client and start downloading and uploading files with peers that were already in the system. Similarly, nodes are often free to leave at any time for any reason. This is already true in distributed systems due to the faulty network, but it's generally assumed that a node will return eventually; in peer-to-peer systems, there is no guarantee that a node will ever return.
With openness also comes lack of trust --- if any device can join the BitTorrent system, the system might need to account for weak devices and actively malicious actors.
TODO maybe say a bit more on that or why we're ignoring it.

Finally, there is no inherent source of truth in peer-to-peer networks. In the traditional clients-and-one-server model, the authoritative copy of data lies with the server. But in a peer to peer network where different nodes may have different versions of some data, there's no architectural difference between the two to decide which node is "right."

All of this means that communication between nodes is inherently prone to failure, meaning that it cannot be completely trusted; and there is always the possibility that a node doesn't have the most up-to-date information.

### Lamport's partial order

Source... @lamport-clock

One challenge of distributed systems is that time is unreliable. On a single processor, there is a relatively clear ordering of events (the order in which the single processor did things). But different machines may or may not have physical clocks, and those clocks may or may not be accurate. Even if they are accurate to human standards, operations on the order of microseconds apart on different machines cannot be easily disentangled into a clear path of what happened first.

To solve this, Leslie Lamport observed that events in a distributed system form a partial order.
TODO Do I need to explain what that is?
On a single machine, there is a total order of operations --- it does $a$, then $b$, then $c$. And another machine may do operations $x$ and $y$. Then the two machines send messages back and forth, which we'll call event $t$. We can confidently say that $a$ happened before $b$, $b$ before $c$, and $c$ before $t$; similarly, $x$ happened before both $y$ and $t$. But there is no inherent way to determine whether $b$ happened sometime before $x$.

### CAP theorem

To explore that last point, say there's some data somehow managed in the distributed system; for example, a list of people who are authorized to access a supercomputer.
The list could be stored by a single machine, or all nodes could store part of the list, or all nodes might have their own copy --- it doesn't matter for the example. But any machine in the distributed system is allowed to make changes to this list.

Now, say that one machine gets an access request and needs to check if the user is authorized, but one of the other nodes has been offline for a while. A decision then has to be made. It's possible that the currently-offline peer has important changes to the access list, so it is reasonable to stall until all peers are available. On the downside, that would mean waiting an indefinite length of time and the user wants to connect right now. So it's also reasonable to go with the most recent information available to the authorizing machine and hope that the offline node doesn't have any relevant pending changes.

Neither of these approaches is incorrect, but each has its benefits and drawbacks. By proceeding without connection, there is the possibility of accessing out-of-date information; by waiting until all peers are available, we indefinitely delay responses. More formally, there are three properties that one might desire from data stored in a distributed system.

Consistency
: every query of the data returns the most up-to-date version or an error. (So we don't get stale data.)

Availability
: every query of the data returns something, regardless of if it's correct. (So we're not hanging forever waiting for a response.)

Partition tolerance
: the system still works with arbitrary partitions of the network. (So we don't crash when one node becomes unreachable.)

Unfortunately, we cannot have all three of these. This is known as the _CAP theorem_, conjectured in @brewer-conjecture and proven in @brewer-proof. It doesn't matter exactly how the data is stored: as long as any node in the system can make changes to it and can also go offline, you cannot guarantee both consistency and availability in the event of a network partition.

There are reasonable critiques of the CAP theorem; see @kleppmann-cap for a good analysis of alternative frameworks.
For one, it relies on a specific definition of consistency --- atomic, linearizable transactions --- and only focuses on a single value to be written. The theorem also says that a system can get both consistency and availability when there is no partition-tolerance; while true, in the real world of distributed systems one always has to design around a network partition in case it occurs.
Furthermore, the CAP theorem does not consider latency at all. If all nodes are reachable but it'll take 20 minutes to get updates, is it worth the wait? Depends on the application and the CAP theorem does not address this question.
But generally speaking, there is usually a tradeoff of availability in distributed systems. Applications that require good availability have to forgo some amount of consistency, whether that's due to latency or partition tolerance.
And the CAP impossibility means there is a large space of options that applications can choose from depending on their needs.

## CRDTs

ADVISE: briefly explain an abstract data type (ADT) and say that. e.g. set ADT. That is an important distinction that I am fluent in but should be made explicit.

TODO add citations to the 2011 Shapiro paper

One solution to the CAP impossibility is a _conflict-free replicated data type_, or CRDT. That is

- a _data type_, e.g. number, list, or tree;
- that is _replicated_, where there are multiple copies of the data on different machines;
- and _conflict-free_, meaning that there is some way of combining copies that always succeeds.

This gets excellent availability and partition-tolerance by just having some local copy of the shared data. Instead of getting perfect consistency, we will settle for _strong eventual consistency_: given enough communication between nodes (when the network is up), all nodes eventually agree upon the final version [@eventual-consistency]. In many applications, this is a reasonable tradeoff: git, for example, doesn't require internet connection while working but only to share and retrieve data from others.

This framework requires a guarantee that different copies of the data will converge to the same value with communication. There are two common ways to ensure this --- either by focusing on the state of the data or the operations applied to it.

### State-based

TODO do I need a source for defining semilattices? I'm just reading off the wikipedia page

ADVISE: put the actual definition in a definition environment. Also link to some textbook, likely "Introduction to Lattices and Order," and use their terminology.

Source... @lattices

State-based CRDTs ensure strong eventual consistency via a join-semilattice over the states. Let $S$ be the set of all possible states of the replicated data, and $\sqcup : S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation (our "join") on $S$. Then $S$ is a join-semilattice via $\sqcup$ if the operation has the following properties for all $x, y, z \in S$:

1. Associativity: $(x \sqcup y) \sqcup z = x \sqcup (y \sqcup z)$. It doesn't matter what order the join is applied in.
2. Commutativity: $x \sqcup y = y \sqcup x.$ There's no "sidedness" to the join.
3. Idempotency: $x \sqcup x = x$. Self-joining does nothing.

This join operation is also called a least upper bound. If these properties hold, then there is always a way to combine two items; furthermore, this combination is minimal in some sense.

<!-- When these conditions are met, both nodes can take the least upper bound of their state and the other. Since it's idempotent, self-merging won't change anything; since it's commutative, the order doesn't matter; and since it's associative, merging three or more states will come out to be the same no matter which we do first. -->

This gives us strong eventual consistency! Given any two copies of some data, we can merge them via the join operation. No matter the order that this propogates throughout the distributed system, if nodes (without making any new changes) keep joining pair-wise then eventually all will have the same state.
So if we can define an operation on our data that has these properties, then we have a CRDT.

<!-- Should I justify these examples? Nah -->
For a simple example, we can easily make a max-number value with state-based power. If our join is the maximum of two real numbers, then our state space $S = \mathbb{R}$. We can verify that this satisfies all the properties: the maximum of any number with itself is itself, and the maximum function does not care about order of inputs or application.
We can also easily make a grow-only set by setting $\sqcup = \cup$ (set union) over all sets. Set union is associative, idempotent, and commutative, meaning this is another CRDT.

### Op-based

ADVISE: I'm really not gonna be focusing on the op-based stuff, but it's here for people to know. I should explicitly say that to the reader.

Operation-based CRDTs achieve strong eventual consistency by requiring that all operations done on the data are commutative: that is, you can apply a collection of operations $a, b, c, \dots$ in any order and the outcome will be the same.
When this is the case, we also get a CRDT.
Nodes share changes by sending out the operations they did as soon as they happened; when a node receives an operation, it simply applies that to its data.
Since we have commutativity, node $A$ doing operation $a$ and then receiving & applying operation $b$ gives the same output as node $B$ doing operation $b$ and then applying the recieved operation $a$.

A simple operation-based CRDT is a number counter with addition (for example a bank account that can be added to or subtracted from). Addition over $\mathbb{R}$ is commutative, so we can represent all operations as $\mathsf{add}(r)$ for some $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and send $r$ to peer nodes. We can also represent a grow-only set using operations: the $\mathsf{add}(s)$ operation which adds an item to a set commutes with all other set additions.

### More complex examples

ADVISE: say "abstract data type" and clean up words. I think this is where I should explain ADTs, the difference between interface and implementation, and what an ordered map/dictionary is.

We've shown two ways to create a grow-only set. What about a "full" set? Only considering two operations, $\mathsf{add}$ and $\mathsf{remove}$ which operate on one item at a time, we immediately encounter a problem: these are not commutative. To illustrate this, consider the three operations $\mathsf{add}(7), \mathsf{add}(7), \mathsf{remove}(7)$. Since sets have no duplicates, the second $\mathsf{add}$ does nothing, and then the $\mathsf{remove}$ removes the $7$, yielding no overall change. But if we $\mathsf{add}(7), \mathsf{remove}(7), \mathsf{add}(7)$, the $\mathsf{add}$ at the end means there is overall a $7$ added to the set.

How can we fix this? It turns out that there is no real way to make a perfect set CRDT due to the above issue. However, we can create reasonable approximations with varying ways to resolve the non-commutativity.

ADVISE: reference the Shapiro paper here

One solution is storing two grow-only sets (called a two-phase or 2P-set), one called the tombstone set. Once an item is added to the tombstone set, it's treated as no longer in the overall set. So they user-facing set equals $A ~\backslash~ T$, where $A$ is the added set and $T$ is the tombstone set. This is easy to implement, since it's just two grow-only sets; however, it doesn't allow for re-adding elements which have already been removed. This could be alleviated to the $n$th degree by having $n$ pairs of added/removed sets in a hierarchy, but that is simply not practical or very useful most of the time.

Another solution is to have an operation-based counter on each item. Internally the set stores an integer for each item observed, and shows the user all items whose counter is greater than zero.
For operations, it'll translate $\mathsf{add}(7)$ into incrementing the counter on $7$ by one. Similarly, $\mathsf{remove}(7)$ will be translated to subtract as many as needed from the $7$ counter to bring it to $0$ --- so if the counter is at $3$, then the underlying operation will be to subtract three from the $7$s counter.
This will not always give desirable, set-like semantics --- a remove operation could feasibly make an item counter negative, meaning an $\mathsf{add}$ wouldn't actually add something to the final represented set. This could be fixed by changing the underlying operation to increment more, but it'll still provide a sometimes-unintuitive experience. It _is_ a way to represent a set as a CRDT though!

Yet another way of getting around the problem is to attach unique identifiers to all items when $\mathsf{add}$ing. We mix this with a 2P-set.
This means $\mathsf{add}(7)$ internally adds $7_\alpha$ to the added set; then $\mathsf{remove}(7)$ will put all observed $7_*$ items into the tombstone set.
With this system, the only underlying operations that don't commute are adding and removing the same item with the same identifier; if we ensure that an application only removes items that it has seen, then all the real-world scenarios commute.
